subtopic_detail: Painless scrotal swelling in a ten month old that transilluminates, has an upper border you can palpate above it, and does not change with crying
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10 month old boy whose mother noticed at bath time that his left side of the scrotum looks bigger than the right. It has been there for at least two months, is the same size in the morning and the evening, and does not change when he cries or strains.

He feeds well, opens his bowels daily, has never vomited and is thriving on the 60th centile. He does not seem to mind when she washes the area. On examination the swelling is soft and non-tender, you can feel normal cord above it, and it lights up when you shine a torch behind it. Both testes are descended and the scrotal skin is normal.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender left scrotal swelling measuring about 3 cm, transilluminates brightly, upper border easily palpable with normal spermatic cord above it, no impulse on crying, no reducibility, both testes palpable within the scrotum, abdomen soft and non-distended, groins without swelling or tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for herniotomy on the next available list
options.rationale: Urgent repair is for an inguinal hernia, which extends into the groin, has no palpable upper border, and characteristically enlarges with crying and reduces when the child is relaxed. The near pair matters because a hernia in this age group carries a real risk of incarceration while this lesion does not. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.text: Arrange a scrotal ultrasound with Doppler before deciding on any referral
options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for a swelling that fails to transilluminate, a testis that cannot be felt separately, or a suspicion of a mass or torsion. Imaging adds nothing when the clinical findings already define the lesion and both testes are palpable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children

options.text: Arrange aspiration of the fluid in the clinic and send it for cell count analysis
options.rationale: Aspiration is not part of paediatric practice because the fluid reaccumulates while the underlying processus remains patent, and the procedure risks injuring the testis. It also converts a benign observation problem into an invasive one. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

options.text: Start a course of oral antibiotics and review the swelling again in one week
options.rationale: Antibiotics would treat epididymo-orchitis, which is painful, tender and often accompanied by fever, dysuria or scrotal erythema. A painless swelling in a well afebrile infant with normal overlying skin has no infective features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Reassure the parents and review him in the clinic after his second birthday
options.rationale: A swelling with a palpable upper border that does not vary in size is a non communicating collection around the testis, and the processus vaginalis closes spontaneously in most infants, so the great majority resolve by two years without any intervention. Surgery is considered only for persistence beyond that age. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions

explanation.summary: Fluid collecting within the tunica vaginalis is common in the first year of life and reflects incomplete obliteration of the processus vaginalis after testicular descent. The clinical task is to separate it from an inguinal hernia, which is the lesion that threatens the bowel and the testis, and the three discriminators are a palpable upper border, transillumination, and whether the swelling changes size with crying or through the day. A collection that fluctuates in size indicates a communication with the peritoneum and behaves more like a hernia, warranting earlier surgical opinion. Persistence beyond two years, rapid enlargement, or the appearance of a new collection in an older boy all justify referral, the last because it may signal an underlying testicular tumour or torsion of an appendage.
key_points: A palpable upper border places the swelling below the inguinal canal
Transillumination indicates fluid rather than bowel within the sac
Size that varies with crying indicates a patent communication
Most non communicating collections resolve before two years of age
A new collection in an older boy warrants ultrasound of the testis
explanation.pearls: A scrotal swelling that is larger at the end of the day and smaller after a night in the cot indicates a communicating processus and should be referred for repair rather than observed, because the same defect can admit bowel.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Inguinal and scrotal conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Scrotal swelling in children

subtopic_detail: Two days of early morning vomiting and afternoon drowsiness in an afebrile child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place since infancy
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 6 year old boy who has vomited on waking for the last two mornings and has complained of a headache each time. His mother says he was his normal self between episodes yesterday, but this afternoon he fell asleep on the couch at four o'clock and has been hard to rouse since.

He had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted at four months for hydrocephalus following a grade three intraventricular haemorrhage of prematurity, and was last revised at age two. He has had no diarrhoea and nobody else at home is unwell. He is afebrile and his neck is supple, with no rash. His pupils are equal and reactive and the optic discs look normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 13 with eye opening to voice, neck supple with no photophobia, pupils 3 mm equal and reactive, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, upgaze appears reduced, shunt reservoir behind the right ear refills slowly after compression, no erythema or swelling along the shunt tract, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L, venous blood gas with normal pH and lactate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Give intravenous ondansetron and observe him in the short stay unit overnight
options.rationale: Antiemetic treatment suits gastroenteritis, which would give diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever or a sick contact, none of which are present. Treating the symptom here removes the only visible sign of a rising intracranial pressure while the pathology continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture for cell count and culture after taking blood cultures
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in suspected obstructive hydrocephalus risks downward herniation, and shunt infection is sampled by neurosurgical tap of the reservoir rather than by the lumbar route. His supple neck, normal temperature and clean shunt tract also argue against infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Give a trial of intranasal sumatriptan and arrange outpatient neurology follow up
options.rationale: Migraine is a diagnosis for a child with a normal conscious state between and during attacks, and it does not progressively reduce the level of consciousness over an afternoon. A first presentation of headache in a shunted child is never assumed to be primary. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Headache

options.text: Arrange an urgent non-contrast computed tomogram of the head and call neurosurgery
options.rationale: Morning headache and vomiting with declining conscious state in a shunted child is shunt failure until proven otherwise, and the imaging that answers it is a rapid non-contrast head scan compared with previous studies for ventricular size, obtained alongside an immediate neurosurgical discussion. Reduced upgaze and a sluggishly refilling reservoir both support raised pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to look for a collection around the distal catheter
options.rationale: An abdominal pseudocyst does cause distal shunt obstruction, but it presents with abdominal distension, pain or a palpable mass, and it is looked for after the head has been imaged. His abdomen is soft and the immediate threat is intracranial. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Around a third of ventriculoperitoneal shunts fail within the first year and the cumulative risk of at least one revision through childhood approaches half. Obstruction is the commonest mode and presents with the classic features of raised intracranial pressure, which in children means headache and vomiting worst on waking, irritability, declining school performance, and eventually drowsiness, impaired upgaze and bradycardia with hypertension. Papilloedema is an unreliable sign because it takes time to develop and is often absent in an acute rise. The standard assessment pairs urgent imaging of the ventricles against a baseline study with a shunt series and early neurosurgical involvement, since definitive treatment is surgical revision.
key_points: Headache and vomiting on waking suggest raised intracranial pressure
Absent papilloedema does not exclude an acute pressure rise
Impaired upgaze reflects pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Compare ventricular size with a previous study, not with a normal range
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when obstruction is suspected
explanation.pearls: A shunt reservoir that refills slowly after compression suggests proximal obstruction and one that is difficult to depress suggests distal obstruction, but neither finding is sensitive enough to exclude failure, so a normal reservoir examination never overrules a convincing history.

subtopic_detail: Alert four month old with profound axial hypotonia, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing who missed newborn screening
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4 month old girl who has never lifted her head and has stopped kicking her legs over the past month. Her parents arrived in Australia from overseas when she was six weeks old, and she did not have a newborn screening test performed in her country of birth.

Her cry is weak and feeds take forty minutes, though she takes the full volume and has gained weight along the 15th centile. Her mother says she watches faces and smiles readily. On the cot she lies with her hips abducted and her arms flat beside her. Her chest draws in as her abdomen rises with each breath, and her tongue shows fine rippling movements at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert with a bright social smile and normal facial expression, profound axial and limb hypotonia with complete head lag on pull to sit, antigravity movement only at the fingers and toes, deep tendon reflexes absent throughout, fine fasciculations of the tongue at rest, bell shaped chest with paradoxical inward movement on inspiration, no organomegaly, no cataracts or coarse features
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units per litre (less than 200), venous blood gas with normal pH and lactate, capillary blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Central causes of hypotonia produce reduced alertness, a poor social response, dysmorphism or seizures, and often upper motor neurone signs. A socially engaged infant with absent reflexes has a lower motor neurone problem, and the anaesthetic itself is hazardous with her respiratory pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the quadriceps with electron microscopy and enzyme histochemistry
options.rationale: Biopsy is directed at a congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophy, which is the near pair here, but those raise the creatine kinase or at least do not spare it entirely and do not produce tongue fasciculations. Genetic testing now precedes biopsy for this phenotype. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

options.text: Targeted genetic testing of the survival motor neurone gene on a blood sample
options.rationale: Alertness with a normal facial expression places the lesion below the brain, and areflexia with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase localises it to the anterior horn cell rather than to muscle or nerve. Deletion testing of the survival motor neurone gene confirms the diagnosis in the great majority and is the test that unlocks disease modifying therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Repeat newborn screening card analysis for metabolic and endocrine disorders
options.rationale: Metabolic causes of hypotonia usually announce themselves with encephalopathy, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, organomegaly or a raised lactate, and her gas and glucose are normal. The screen is worth completing for public health reasons but it will not explain a pure motor picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness

options.text: Repetitive nerve stimulation study with acetylcholine receptor antibody measurement
options.rationale: Neuromuscular junction disease gives fatigable weakness with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia and characteristically preserves the deep tendon reflexes. Her reflexes are absent and her eye movements are full, which points away from the junction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

explanation.summary: The floppy infant is sorted first into central and peripheral causes, and the single most useful bedside discriminator is the level of alertness and social interaction, because a baby who engages normally while lying motionless has a problem below the brain. Within the peripheral group, absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations and a normal creatine kinase indicate anterior horn cell degeneration, while a raised creatine kinase points to muscle and distal sensory loss points to nerve. Australian newborn bloodspot screening has included the survival motor neurone gene since 2022, so infants born here are usually identified presymptomatically, and a symptomatic presentation now most often means the child was born elsewhere or predates the programme. Diagnosis is urgent because disease modifying therapies work best before motor neurones are lost, and respiratory and nutritional support must be organised in parallel.
key_points: Preserved alertness with profound weakness indicates a peripheral cause
Absent reflexes with tongue fasciculations localise to the anterior horn cell
A normal creatine kinase argues against a primary muscle disorder
Paradoxical breathing reflects intercostal weakness with a spared diaphragm
Genetic confirmation is urgent because treatment is time critical
explanation.pearls: Intercostal weakness with diaphragm sparing produces the bell shaped chest and inward chest movement on inspiration, and these infants decompensate abruptly during minor viral illness, so respiratory review and a cough assist plan should be arranged before the first winter.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Floppy infant and weakness
BMJ Best Practice: Spinal muscular atrophy

subtopic_detail: Toddler with a harsh brassy cough and noisy breathing since infancy that worsens with crying and has not responded to eight weeks of inhaled therapy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 14 month old boy whose parents describe noisy breathing since about three months of age and a cough they call barking or brassy. The noise is loudest when he is crying, feeding or running about, and it almost disappears when he is asleep and settled.

He was born at term, has never been intubated, and has no eczema and no family history of asthma. He is on the 50th centile for weight and has never been admitted. A trial of salbutamol through a spacer made no difference, and eight weeks of a low dose inhaled corticosteroid has not changed anything. Between episodes his chest sounds clear, and during them you hear a single pitched noise in expiration over the central chest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Harsh brassy cough on request, monophonic expiratory wheeze loudest over the trachea and central chest, no inspiratory stridor at rest, chest clear with normal air entry when settled, no chest wall deformity or Harrison sulci, no clubbing, growth along the 50th centile, cardiovascular examination normal with no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal lung fields with a normal cardiac silhouette and no right sided aortic arch

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric respiratory service for flexible bronchoscopy of the airway
options.rationale: A brassy cough with a central monophonic wheeze that varies with effort and settles in sleep describes dynamic collapse of a large airway, which is diagnosed by looking at the airway during spontaneous breathing. Flexible bronchoscopy both confirms the collapse and excludes an intraluminal lesion or extrinsic compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.text: Increase the inhaled corticosteroid dose and add a long acting beta agonist now
options.rationale: Escalating preventer therapy assumes asthma, which gives polyphonic wheeze scattered through both lung fields, atopy, and at least partial bronchodilator response. He has none of these and has already failed an adequate eight week trial. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Arrange a rigid bronchoscopy on the emergency list for removal of a foreign body
options.rationale: An inhaled foreign body causes abrupt symptoms in a previously well child, usually with a witnessed choking episode and unilateral signs or hyperinflation on the film. Symptoms present since three months of age and a normal radiograph do not fit. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

options.text: Start a two week course of oral amoxicillin and clavulanate for a wet cough now
options.rationale: Extended antibiotics treat protracted bacterial bronchitis, the near pair for chronic cough in this age group, but that cough is wet and productive rather than brassy and it is not positional or effort dependent. A dry barking cough with a monophonic noise is mechanical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Arrange a twenty four hour oesophageal pH study and start a proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: Reflux can aggravate airway symptoms and coexists with large airway collapse, but it is not the primary explanation for a noise that changes with respiratory effort and disappears in sleep. Treating it first leaves the structural question unanswered. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Tracheomalacia)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Tracheomalacia

explanation.summary: Not every wheezing toddler has asthma, and the pattern of the noise is the key to the alternatives. Polyphonic wheeze scattered through both fields with a bronchodilator response indicates small airway disease, while a single pitched noise heard loudest centrally indicates one large airway that is narrowing. Dynamic collapse of the trachea or a main bronchus classically causes a brassy or barking cough, noise that worsens with crying, feeding and exertion and improves with rest, and complete failure to respond to inhaled therapy. The differential includes extrinsic compression by a vascular ring or a mediastinal mass, which is why the airway is examined directly and the arch anatomy is checked before the symptoms are attributed to a benign floppy trachea that will improve through the second and third years.
key_points: Monophonic central wheeze indicates a single large airway, not small airways
A brassy barking cough with effort dependent noise suggests dynamic collapse
Failure of an adequate preventer trial should prompt review of the diagnosis
Flexible bronchoscopy during spontaneous breathing shows the collapse
Exclude extrinsic vascular compression before accepting a benign cause
explanation.pearls: A toddler whose noisy breathing is worse when lying prone and better when lying on the side, and whose cough is brassy rather than wet, should be referred before a third preventer escalation, because inhaled corticosteroid has no effect on a collapsing airway and delays the structural diagnosis by months.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Stridor and noisy breathing

subtopic_detail: Head circumference crossing two centile lines between three and seven months with a full fontanelle in a developmentally normal infant
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a 7 month check on a boy who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother has no concerns and he sits with a straight back, transfers a block between his hands and babbles.

His head circumference was on the 50th centile at birth and the 50th at three months, and today it plots on the 97th. His length and weight remain on the 50th. His anterior fontanelle feels full when he is sitting quietly and not crying, and the skull sutures feel slightly separated at the coronal suture. His eyes move fully in all directions and he fixes and follows. Both parents have head circumferences on the 50th centile for adults.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 97th centile having tracked the 50th at birth and at three months, anterior fontanelle full but not tense at rest, slight separation of the coronal suture, scalp veins not distended, no setting sun sign with full upgaze, red reflexes present and symmetrical, tone and reflexes normal, sits unsupported and transfers objects, no organomegaly, no bruising

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure both parents' head circumferences and plot a repeat measurement monthly
options.rationale: Familial large head is a valid explanation for a head that is large but growing parallel to a centile line, and the parental measurements here are ordinary. A head that crosses centiles is describing a rate of growth, which no family history can normalise. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with sedation as the first study
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the better test for posterior fossa detail and is appropriate once ultrasound is abnormal or the fontanelle has closed, so the near pair question is sequence rather than suitability. Starting here commits an infant to sedation for information a bedside study can provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly

options.text: Arrange skull radiographs to assess the sutures for premature fusion and ridging
options.rationale: Premature suture fusion produces an abnormally shaped head with a palpable ridge and a head circumference that falls away rather than accelerates, because the skull cannot expand. His sutures are separated, which is the opposite finding. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Macrocephaly)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Macrocephaly

options.text: Reassure the parents that development is normal and repeat the plot in three months
options.rationale: Normal development is genuinely reassuring about the past but says nothing about a process still expanding, and infants compensate for raised pressure by enlarging the skull until they suddenly do not. Waiting three months risks presenting later with vomiting and impaired upgaze. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly

options.text: Arrange a cranial ultrasound through the fontanelle within the next few days
options.rationale: Crossing two centile lines with a full fontanelle and separating sutures requires imaging rather than observation, and while the fontanelle remains open an ultrasound shows ventricular size and extra-axial fluid without radiation or sedation. It separates enlarged subarachnoid spaces from progressive ventricular dilatation, which need different follow up. (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly

explanation.summary: Head circumference is interpreted as a trajectory rather than as a single point, and the finding that demands action is crossing centile lines upward, particularly with signs of raised pressure such as a full fontanelle, separated sutures, distended scalp veins or impaired upgaze. The commonest benign explanation in this age group is enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces, which typically runs in families, presents with a rapidly enlarging but soft head, and resolves by two years with normal development. Progressive hydrocephalus from aqueduct stenosis, a posterior fossa lesion or a chronic subdural collection all present identically at the start, and a subdural collection additionally raises the question of inflicted injury. Cranial ultrasound through an open fontanelle is the practical first study in Australian primary care, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for abnormal or equivocal findings.
key_points: Crossing upward through centile lines matters more than the absolute centile
A full fontanelle and separated sutures indicate raised intracranial pressure
Familial macrocephaly grows parallel to a centile line rather than crossing
Ultrasound through an open fontanelle avoids sedation and radiation
Normal development does not exclude an actively expanding process
explanation.pearls: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces carries a genuinely increased risk of subdural haemorrhage after trivial trauma, so a subdural collection found in an infant with this finding does not by itself resolve the question of inflicted injury and still warrants a full safeguarding assessment.

subtopic_detail: Six week old breastfed infant with a bulging fontanelle and bruising whose parents declined the birth injection, with prolonged clotting times and a normal platelet count
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 6 week old boy brought in because he has been irritable all day, has vomited three times and has gone pale. His mother says he has fed poorly since this morning and has had one brief episode where his right arm and leg jerked for about a minute.

He was born at home at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and is fully breastfed. His parents declined the injection offered to him after birth and he has had no vitamin supplements. There is no history of a fall or any other injury. He has a bruise at the site where blood was taken twenty minutes ago and a soft bulge of the anterior fontanelle when he is held upright.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and irritable with a high pitched cry, anterior fontanelle bulging when held upright, no neck stiffness and no rash, oozing from the venepuncture site with surrounding bruising, no retinal haemorrhage seen on limited examination, no bony tenderness or deformity, liver edge 1 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (100-140), platelets 388 x10^9/L (150-450), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), international normalised ratio 6.4 (0.9-1.3), activated partial thromboplastin time 92 seconds (25-38), fibrinogen 2.9 g/L (1.5-4.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a platelet transfusion now and arrange urgent computed tomography of the head
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion treats thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, and his count is squarely normal at 388. Transfusing platelets into a factor deficiency corrects nothing and delays the treatment that does. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K now and arrange urgent computed tomography of the head
options.rationale: A prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen is the signature of deficient vitamin K dependent factors, and in a breastfed infant who received no prophylaxis this is late haemorrhagic disease with intracranial bleeding until imaged. Replacing the vitamin corrects the underlying defect within hours while the scan defines the bleed. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.text: Give intravenous cefotaxime now and perform a lumbar puncture once he is stable
options.rationale: Meningitis is the standard reflex for an irritable infant with a bulging fontanelle, but he is afebrile with a normal C reactive protein, and lumbar puncture with an international normalised ratio of 6.4 risks a spinal haematoma. The coagulation profile is the disconfirming finding that redirects the whole assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma alone and arrange urgent computed tomography of the head
options.rationale: Plasma is a useful adjunct for immediate factor replacement in life threatening bleeding and is given alongside the vitamin, so the near pair question is what corrects the deficiency rather than what fills the gap. Plasma alone wears off within hours because the liver still cannot carboxylate the factors. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey now and refer to the child protection unit before treatment
options.rationale: Inflicted injury must be considered in any infant with intracranial bleeding, and the assessment proceeds, but it does not precede treatment and it does not explain a grossly deranged coagulation profile with normal platelets. Correct the coagulopathy first and keep the safeguarding question open. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Child abuse

explanation.summary: Vitamin K dependent factors two, seven, nine and ten fall over the first weeks of life because placental transfer is poor, the gut is not yet colonised and breast milk contains very little vitamin K, which is why a single intramuscular dose is offered to every Australian newborn. The late form of the deficiency presents between two and twelve weeks, almost exclusively in breastfed infants who missed prophylaxis or who have unrecognised cholestasis, and roughly half of these infants present with intracranial haemorrhage. The laboratory signature is a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen, which separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation and from thrombocytopenic causes. Treatment is intravenous vitamin K with plasma or prothrombin complex for active major bleeding, alongside imaging and neurosurgical involvement.
key_points: Late presentation occurs between two and twelve weeks in breastfed infants
Prolonged clotting times with normal platelets and fibrinogen is the signature
Intracranial haemorrhage is the presentation in about half of late cases
Intravenous vitamin K corrects the defect, plasma only bridges it
Lumbar puncture is unsafe until the coagulopathy has been corrected
explanation.pearls: An infant with this presentation who has also had pale stools or prolonged jaundice needs a conjugated bilirubin measured on the same admission, because biliary atresia causes fat malabsorption and can produce the identical deficiency despite a correctly given birth dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, paediatrics
